headline: Halfway Rock mackerel thick, bass still feeding in daylight while the coast goes dark
subhead: Cool Gulf of Maine water is keeping Casco Bay's bite honest through July while stripers south of the Cape slide nocturnal.
body_markdown:
I was off Halfway Rock Wednesday morning, engine idling, watching the surface go nervous the way it does when mackerel are pushed up tight from below. Terns working, then diving, then working again — that steady rhythm you learn to read after enough summers out there. It's the kind of thing you could set a lecture on: predictable, if you know what to look for. And this week the bay is giving us plenty to look at.

Mackerel are thick from the Rock down to Cape Small right now, schools stacking in that 20-to-40-foot band over structure, and they're pulling striped bass up onto the ledges to feed on them. That's the story of this week, and it's a good one, because south of us — the Sound, the Jersey beaches, even down around the Cape — warming water has pushed bass into a mostly nocturnal pattern. Kings Point was reading better than 71 degrees earlier this week, warm enough that bass down there are backing off daylight feeding and holding to current breaks after dark. We don't have that problem here. The Gulf of Maine keeps pumping cooler water into Casco Bay, and our stripers are still feeding hard in full daylight, right on schedule, right where you'd expect them.

Best of it has been on the back side of Peaks Island and along the Bailey Island ledges, particularly Card Cove and the rips off Elm Point, on the last two hours of the ebb into the start of the flood. That current swing pulls bait off the ledges and bass tuck in behind the drop to ambush it. I've been running a 2-ounce diamond jig, no tube, straight bucktail hook, dropped to the bottom and worked with a slow sweeping lift — nothing fancy, just enough action to look like a mackerel losing the fight against the current. Fish have been running 24 to 30 inches mostly, with a few better ones mixed in on the deeper drop-offs, 35 to 45 feet, where the ledge falls away sharply on the Bailey Island side.

Halfway Rock itself has been steady for groundfish — cod and haddock both — but it's a slack-tide game out there and you need to respect it. The Rock sits in enough current that fishing anything but the slack window, roughly 45 minutes either side of the tide change, means you're mostly fighting your own line instead of working bottom. In that window, jigging diamond jigs or bucktails tipped with a strip of mackerel belly in 90 to 120 feet has been putting cod in the 4-to-8-pound range in the boat, with haddock mixed in on the sandier patches to the northeast of the Rock. It's not a blitz — call it steady, worth the run, but you're earning every fish with good bottom contact and patience through the drift.

Bluefish have started showing as strays around Two Lights and the outer edge of Casco Bay, which lines up with what we flagged last week — that bluefish would keep following bait schools north along the coast as the warm water pushes incrementally further up the Gulf of Maine each season. We're not talking blitz conditions like they're seeing further south with the bunker schools, just occasional choppers mixed in with the mackerel runs, but it's worth keeping a wire leader rigged if you're jigging the outer ledges, because losing a diamond jig to a blue's teeth stings less than losing a good striper rig.

I'll be honest about one thing — the inner harbor bite around Portland itself has been spotty this week. A lot of small bait, a lot of bass moving through, but nothing holding station long enough to make it worth more than a passing cast on your way out to the islands. If you've only got an hour, skip the harbor and run straight for the ledges.

Looking ahead, we're easing toward the first quarter moon on the 21st, which means the tide swings are softening from the spring tides we had around the new moon last week. Slower current usually means the ledge bite mellows a touch — fish don't get pinned as hard against structure — but it also means a more forgiving window if you're new to fishing these ledges, since you won't be fighting a five-knot rip to hold bottom at the Rock. If the mackerel schools hold through the weekend, and there's no reason to think they won't with water temps staying comfortable in the mid-to-high 50s at depth, I'd expect the Bailey Island and Peaks Island bass bite to carry right through into next week. My money's on an early morning tide at Card Cove Saturday, working the last of the ebb with a diamond jig worked slow along the bottom edge. That's where I'll be.
